title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, and Incident Response — Control Framework
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary:
This document defines Redwood Inference’s canonical controls and operational procedures for role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging and retention, data residency and retention policies, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) gates, incident response for security events, compliance evidence collection workflows, and the risk/exception process. It is intended for engineering, security, and compliance stakeholders who implement, operate, or validate controls.

Goals:
- Enforce least-privilege access across cloud, console, and service accounts.
- Maintain immutable, searchable audit logs with defined retention and access controls.
- Ensure customer and internal data is stored and processed in allowed regions with documented retention schedules.
- Integrate security gates into the SDLC to reduce production vulnerabilities.
- Provide a repeatable incident response process for security events with forensics and customer notification steps.
- Centralize evidence and ownership for audits and certifications.

1) RBAC & Authentication (AuthN/AuthZ)
Overview:
Redwood uses centralized identity provider (IdP) SSO for human accounts and managed secrets for service identity. All interactive user authentication is via Okta (SSO). Service identities use short-lived AWS/IAM roles or mTLS-enabled service principals for on-prem components.

Principles and controls:
- Principle of least privilege: grant the minimum set of permissions required.
- Role-first model: define roles (job function) and map Okta groups to cloud and application roles via SCIM and AWS IAM role mappings.
- No local passwords: console/API access for humans must be via SSO; local account creation is disallowed except for emergency break-glass (see exceptions).
- MFA required: Adaptive MFA enforced for all interactive users; hardware 2nd factor enforced for privileged roles.
- Service accounts: short-lived credentials (assume-role) preferred; long-lived credentials must be approved and stored in Vault with automatic rotation.
- Privileged access reviews: quarterly review of all role memberships and privileged IAM roles.
- Access request workflow: requests opened in JIRA with justification, owner approval, and automatic expiry.

Role matrix (summary):
| Role | Typical members | Scope | Typical privileges | Review cadence |
|------|-----------------|-------|--------------------|----------------|
| Platform-Admin | SRE, Infra Eng | Organization-wide (non-production & production) | IAM, VPC, KMS key management | Monthly for on-call; quarterly otherwise |
| Service-Owner | Product/Service Eng | Service namespace | Deploy, rollback, config change | Quarterly |
| Read-Only-Audit | Security, Compliance | Org-wide read access | View logs, configurations | Annually |
| Developer | Application teams | Dev/staging namespaces | Deploy to dev, raise PRs | Quarterly |

SSO & provisioning:
- IdP: Okta — SAML/OIDC for web consoles, SCIM for group provisioning to GitHub and internal apps.
- Cloud federation: AWS SSO/AssumeRole configured per-account with role mappings.
- SCIM provisioning with group-to-role mapping is the canonical source for non-entitlement attributes.
- SCIM provisioning and role mappings are owned by the IAM team (infra).

Service accounts and secrets:
- Vault (HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager depending on environment) is the canonical secret store.
- Service tokens must be scoped and have TTL <= 24 hours unless exception approved.
- Automated rotation: secrets used by long-running services must have rotation jobs and CI checks that fail deployments if rotation is overdue.

2) Audit Logging
What we log:
- Authentication events (login, MFA challenges, SSO assertions).
- API calls to control plane (model deployments, capacity changes, role changes).
- Administrative actions (KMS key creation/rotation, IAM policy changes).
- Configuration changes to infrastructure (Terraform state changes, pipeline run changes).
- Access to sensitive customer data endpoints (reads/writes), and service account usage.
- Detection alerts (IDS/EDR) and significant system errors.

Log pipeline and retention:
- Agents: application and runtime logs are forwarded via fluentd to central log ingestion.
- Aggregation: primary aggregation in Datadog Logs; security audit stream forwarded to Splunk (indexed) for long-term retention and immutable WORM storage for evidentiary data.
- Immutable archives: critical audit logs (IAM changes, KMS operations, customer-data access) are copied to an S3 bucket with Object Lock (governance mode) and KMS encryption (arn:aws:kms:region:acct:key/REDACTED) for 7 years unless regulatory requirements dictate longer retention.
- Retention schedules (default):
  - Operational logs (Datadog): 90 days hot, 1 year cold.
  - Security audit logs (Splunk/WORM): 7 years.
  - Application request traces (APM): 90 days.
  - Customer request payloads / content: retention per customer SLA (see Data Residency & Retention section).

Access & monitoring:
- Access to raw audit logs restricted to Read-Only-Audit role plus explicit allow lists; all queries are logged.
- Alerts: anomalous IAM policy changes, service account creation, and unexpected cross-account assume-role events generate PagerDuty incidents (P1/P2 based on scope).

3) Data Residency & Retention
Data classification categories:
- PII/Customer Data: identifiable user content and outputs.
- System Logs: telemetry and operational traces.
- Audit Trail: IAM and admin events.

Region controls:
- Hosted data regions are declared per-customer in contract; production customer content must not leave selected region(s) except with written customer consent.
- Region enforcement: infrastructure-level placement via Terraform (region-scoped resources), and a policy engine (policy-as-code) that blocks non-compliant deployments in CI.

Retention schedules (examples):
- Customer request payloads: default 30 days (hosted); configurable per-customer SLA (30/90/365).
- Embeddings/derived vectors: retained only if customer opt-in; default 90 days.
- Audit logs: 7 years (see Audit Logging).
- Backups (DB snapshots): 90 days unless longer retention mandated.

Data deletion and egress:
- Deletion workflow: documented delete request procedure that asynchronously deletes data and emits an audit event.
- Egress approvals: any cross-region or external transfer of customer data requires Security and Legal approval and an entry in the data transfer register.
- Verification: after deletion, run verification job to confirm object removal and record checksums in audit log.

4) Secure SDLC (Security Gates & Tooling)
Pipeline & tools:
- Source control: GitHub (org: redwood-inference). Branch protection, required status checks.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions and self-hosted runners for GPU jobs.
- Static analysis: Dependabot and Snyk for dependency vulnerability scanning; secret scanning enabled at repo-level.
- SAST/DAST: periodic SAST runs on critical services; DAST scans for public-facing services.
- IaC scanning: Checkov/terrascan for Terraform and policy checks in PRs.

Gates and requirements for production rollout:
- All PRs require at least one code review and passing CI checks.
- Security checks: no high/critical Snyk vulnerabilities allowed in production dependencies unless an approved mitigation plan exists.
- Automated tests: unit, integration, and smoke tests required; performance benchmark must be within service SLO.
- Dependency approval: new base images and major dependency upgrades require Security review.

Threat modeling and design reviews:
- Threat modeling required for new services handling customer data or new public endpoints.
- Design review checklist: data flows, auth model, failure modes, mitigations, and monitoring. Document in PR and link to Confluence design spec.

Release notes and changelogs:
- Every production change must include a changelog entry and rollout plan with rollback steps in the release ticket.

5) Incident Response — Security Events
Overview:
This section defines the runbook for security incidents (unauthorized access, data exfiltration, major vulnerability exploitation, compromise of secrets). Operational incident runbooks (oncall-and-incident-response) contain playbooks for specific services.

High-level process:
1. Detection & Triage
   - Tools: IDS/EDR alerts, Splunk/SIEM detections, Datadog anomaly alerts, and third-party reports.
   - Triage owner: Alert routed to oncall SRE and security oncall.
2. Classify & Escalate
   - Severity classification (S1–S4) based on data exposure, service impact, and customer impact.
   - P1 (S1): confirmed exfiltration of customer data or active compromise of production keys; immediate incident commander (IC) assignment and PagerDuty page.
3. Containment
   - Short-term: revoke compromised keys/assume-role sessions, isolate affected instances (network ACLs, security groups), apply firewall rules.
   - Medium-term: rotate secrets, deploy hotfix, and cut traffic using routing policies.
4. Forensics & Root Cause
   - Preserve evidence: snapshot affected instances to forensic S3 bucket with Object Lock. Document chain-of-custody.
   - Capture memory if needed, collect relevant logs (secure-copy to forensics store), and store checksums in audit trail.
5. Remediation & Recovery
   - Implement fixes, validate via tests, and restore service.
   - Post-incident monitoring window (30 days) with elevated sampling and additional alerts.
6. Communication & Reporting
   - Internal: initial incident summary within 1 hour, detailed timeline within 24 hours.
   - External: customer notification within SLA terms and legal guidance; regulator notification when required by law.
7. Post-incident review
   - Postmortem published within 7 business days; include root cause, timeline, mitigations, and action items with owners and due dates.

Evidence & legal preservation:
- Security incidents that may implicate legal/regulatory obligations require immediate preservation notice to Legal and Compliance.
- Evidence packages compiled in a locked Confluence page and stored artifacts in forensics S3 with restricted ACLs.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows
Audit preparation:
- Controls register: map controls to evidence artifacts (logs, runbooks, screenshots, configuration exports). Maintain mapping in the compliance tracker spreadsheet owned by Compliance.
- Evidence owners: each control has an assigned evidence owner (team) responsible for collecting artifacts on request.

On-demand evidence collection:
- Standard request: a JIRA audit ticket with list of controls; evidence owners respond with links to documents or attach export files.
- Evidence types: policy documents, role membership exports, KMS key rotation logs, signed runbooks, immutable log exports.
- Time-to-provide SLA: 5 business days for standard evidence; 24–48 hours for prioritized regulator requests.

Snapshot & recurring evidence:
- Quarterly evidence snapshots for major controls (RBAC membership exports, IAM policy lists, KMS rotation logs).
- Annual certification evidence package prepared for auditors with runbook links and archived exports.

Evidence storage and protection:
- Canonical evidence stored in the compliance bucket (S3) with restricted access and object immutability for audit artifacts.
- Metadata: every evidence artifact must include provenance fields in its filename: control-id, date, owner.

7) Risk & Exceptions
Exception process:
1. Request: submit exception request via JIRA Security-Exceptions project with risk justification, duration, and compensating controls.
2. Assessment: Security reviews request within 3 business days and assigns a risk rating (Low/Medium/High).
3. Approvals: exceptions for High risk require Security Director + Legal sign-off; Low/Medium may be approved by Security Manager.
4. Mitigation & monitoring: approved exceptions must include compensating controls (extra logging, shortened duration, manual reviews).
5. Renewal: every exception has an expiry (max 90 days for High, 180 days for Medium, 365 days for Low). Renewal requires re-assessment.

Risk acceptance board:
- Membership: Security, Infra, Product, Legal.
- Cadence: weekly triage and monthly formal reviews for outstanding exceptions.

Auditability & metrics:
- Maintain an exceptions register with status, approver, compensating controls, and next review date.
- KPIs: number of active exceptions, average time to approval, percent renewed/closed on time.
